strengths: This article is well-written and easy to understand.
It leverages the semantic alignment strengths of CLIP to enhance the quality of images generated by GANs.
By analyzing text to identify entities, attributes, and relationships, the model can generate images that are not only visually appealing but also semantically consistent with the input text.

The proposed model achieves visually good performance of text-to-image synthesis. This establishes a strong and relatively light-weight GAN baseline in the task which is dominated by heavy diffusion models with much longer sampling time.
The improvement over the baseline GALIP is visible in both FID (image quality) and CLIP score (text-image alignment).
The design of using structural-semantic prompts for better and more consistent visual features is somewhat reasonable.
weaknesses: The experiments are not sufficient to prove the effectiveness of the method in the paper.
Compared with the GALIP paper, there is a lack of comparison results of Model Param and Data Size.
Compared with the GigaGAN paper, there is a lack of comparison results of high-resolution generation.
The main concern is the effectiveness of the proposed designs.
As shown in the ablation study of Table 3, the results are not convincing for me.

For example, comparing '+Hierarchical Semantic Prompts (6)' and '+Hierarchical Semantic Prompts (6), +Prompt CLIP Adaptor', it seems Prompt CLIP Adaptor can only improve the FID by 0.09, CS by 0.0011, which is very marginal and could be neglected considering the seed randomness.
Besides, it seems '+Hard Mining Matching-Aware Loss' can improve the baseline by the 0.33 FID and 0.0024 CS.
But when applying it to a stronger model '+Hierarchical Semantic Prompts (6), +Prompt CLIP Adaptor', the FID and CS can still be improved 0.31 FID and 0.0022.
It is not convincing for me as the improvement should be clearly narrowed with a stronger base model.
The whole paper dives deep into technical implementation of the proposed method, but lacks high-level explanations and discussions of contributions.

The paper does not answer high-level questions such as the key issues with prior GAN-based text-to-image methods, why the proposed method is the most efficient way to address them, possible alternatives for the proposed extensions, and limitations of using all the pre-trained modules.
The paper is full of typos, and non-standard terminology.
The related work section discusses GAN inversion, which is unrelated, and lacks discussion of other text-to-image GAN and diffusion models.
It is not clear what kind of technical novelty the paper presents; the method builds on an existing baseline GALIP and combines existing modules without clear analysis of challenges.
The claim that the loss can be generalized to apply to most generation methods involving semantic matching is unsupported by experiments.
The visual results in the paper are limited (4 images in the main paper and 2 in the supplementary).
The new model achieves somewhat better FID and CLIP scores but works noticeably slower (e.g., 0.025s vs 0.017s in Fig. 1), and the efficiency trade-offs are not discussed.
The manuscript is full of grammar, spelling, punctuation errors and unnatural expressions, making it hard to understand.
The authors provide few qualitative comparisons between their method and baselines; the experiment section should present more synthesized images.
The quantitative results show only minor improvements in FID and CLIP score, which do not reflect the emphasized semantic alignment.
